item.title: Tafoya makes 'common sense' pitch to disaffected Democrats as she vows to fight Minnesota’s ‘socialist lurch’
item.description: Michele Tafoya won the Minnesota GOP Senate primary and now faces Peggy Flanagan, pitching common sense to voters across the political spectrum.
item.content:encoded:
EDINA, MN - As socialist candidates continue to score victories across the country and take more control of the Democratic Party, Minnesota GOP Senate nominee Michele Tafoya is making her pitch to voters from all parties who still believe in "common sense."

"We do not want to see a socialist lurch anywhere in this country, and in particular in Minnesota, so I will do whatever I can to stand up against this movement toward Democrat socialism," Tafoya told Fox News Digital on Tuesday shortly after voting in a suburb outside Minneapolis. "Socialism does not work."

"There is absolutely a home for every voter in Minnesota that wants common sense, that wants a return to sanity, that wants to see kids learn in school again, that wants accountability for this fraud, who wants the fraud never repeat itself, who wants crime rates to go down again," Tafoya told Fox News Digital. "There is room for you. We are the common sense candidacy and we're gonna represent a lot more than just conservatives in this state."

Hours later, Tafoya went from Republican Senate candidate to Republican Senate nominee as she convincingly won her primary and moves on to face Minnesota Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in the general election in November.

MINNESOTA HOUSE SPEAKER LISA DEMUTH WINS GOP GUBERNATORIAL PRIMARY TO REPLACE TIM WALZ IN NOVEMBER

When reached by phone after her victory, Tafoya reiterated her commitment to crossing party lines to reach disaffected Democrats.

"Our state has been going in the wrong direction at the speed of sound and people who love Minnesota are brokenhearted and we see that this has happened under the watch of career politicians single-party rule for many years now they've brought us to this place it's time for change and I think we're going to appeal to voters across the political spectrum to stand up and say we're not going to continue to re-elect the people that got us to this place to begin with," Tafoya told Fox News Digital.

FAILED PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATE WINS DEM PRIMARY FOR MIDWEST GOVERNOR AMID FRAUD SCANDAL FALLOUT

Tafoya is aiming to become the first Republican to win statewide office in Minnesota since 2006.

Tafoya's opponent in November, progressive Minnesota Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, has drawn criticism over the massive fraud scandal in the state that forced Gov. Tim Walz to drop his re-election bid, given that she served alongside him since 2019, as well as her far-left positions that include abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

"It is time to hold them accountable and we're going to do that by firing them," Tafoya said. "And we're gonna hire people who are outsiders, who are willing to come in and fix this with new ideas and not just bend to party politics as the establishment always does."

Tafoya, whose message to disaffected Democrat voters is similar to the pitch Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers made last week in his race against his opponent Abdul El-Sayed, told Fox News Digital she is looking forward to speaking to Democrats and independents in the coming months.

"When you run in a primary, you're talking to mostly your own voters," Tafoya said. "Now I'm excited to reach out to those disaffected Democrats who feel that the party has left them, who feel like they're homeless politically. We're gonna open the doors to them and I can't wait to talk to all those independents and share their ideas So that's what I'm looking forward to."

item.title: Foster Griffin gives Cleveland Guardians the edge in American League Central division matchup
item.description: Foster Griffin's ace-level stats give the Cleveland Guardians an edge against Framber Valdez in this American League Central Division pitching matchup.
item.content:encoded:
Only one baseball play from me yesterday, but it was a winner. Dylan Cease remained in control of the Boston Red Sox, and that hot streak they've been having has now turned into a cold streak. Still, the Red Sox will take suffering four straight losses after winning something around 80% of their games over the past couple of months. We will stay in the American League for today's game, but it will come in a Central Division battle.

The Cleveland Guardians were one of the better teams in the division for a while, but they seem to have lost their luster. They are 58-62 for the season and are 30-31 on the road. Maybe that's what the Guardians are: an average team. They did make some moves at the deadline to bolster an already strong rotation. However, it still seems like this team is always in need of another bat or two to make the lineup more potent. In fairness, they can hit homers and do hit for average, but it just never seems like they are one of the best offensive teams.

Today, they send out one of those deadline deals to the mound in the form of Foster Griffin. He's had a special year after coming back from the Japanese league. For the season, Griffin is 12-4 with a 3.31 ERA and a 1.11 WHIP. Additionally, he has 122 strikeouts for the season. Those numbers are all Ace-level, or at least similar to a second starter. He wasn't great with the Guardians in his first start, giving up five earned runs in four innings on seven hits. Those hits included two homers. That seems to be the main way to score off of Griffin — he's only allowed 54 runs this season, and at least 21 have come off of home runs.

TARIK SKUBAL SAYS HE WAS EMOTIONAL LEAVING DETROIT TIGERS FOR LA DODGERS, WOULD LOVE TO RETURN: 'I'M CRYING'

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

You probably won't be aware of this considering the major news around the Tigers was about trading away the best pitcher in baseball, but they've been surprisingly great this season. That is, if you remove the month of May from their record. In May, the team went 6-22, one of the worst records in baseball. Outside of that, they've been 53-38, which is good for a .582 winning percentage. Only five teams in baseball have a better winning percentage than that currently. The Red Sox don't even have that high of a percentage, and they just had their best stretch in history.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

The Tigers will send out their offseason addition, intended to soften the blow when they traded away Tarik Skubal. They added Framber Valdez to the rotation, and it has been a bit of mixed results this season. He is 7-7 with a 4.17 ERA and a 1.37 WHIP for the year. Valdez had a terrible July, but his first two starts in August have been very strong with just two earned runs allowed in 14 innings. He faced Cleveland once this season, allowing four earned runs over five innings.

What is the way to beat Griffin? It is to hit homers. Which is something that the Tigers are at least decent at. They are 12th in the league in home runs, but a lot of that power seems to go away when they hit against a left-handed pitcher like Griffin. The Tigers have never faced Griffin before, and I think he gives the Guardians the edge here. Give me Cleveland to win this game.

item.description: Legend Storer, a former Concordia University Irvine swimmer, was allegedly naked when he is accused of attacking a Maui, Hawaii resort security guard found dead later.
item.content:encoded:
A former California college swimmer was naked when he allegedly attacked a graveyard shift security guard who was found dead hours later at a Maui, Hawaii resort, authorities said.

Legend Storer, 20, has been charged with second-degree murder, first-degree burglary involving a dangerous instrument and indecent exposure in connection with the Aug. 5 death of Michael "Mike" Dyer, 63, according to court records obtained by Fox News Digital.

The Maui Police Department said the bizarre chain of events began around 1:45 a.m., when surveillance footage captured an unclothed man approaching Dyer’s office at a condominium resort on Lower Honoapiʻilani Road in Lahaina.

Just over an hour later, at about 3:02 a.m., dispatchers received a report of a nude man wandering through a neighborhood in nearby Kahana.

Officers tracked down the unclothed 20-year-old around 3:35 a.m. and found that he had suffered numerous abrasions, police said. He was taken to Maui Memorial Medical Center for evaluation.

Then, at 5:31 a.m., police were called to the resort after Dyer was found unresponsive. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Investigators reviewing surveillance footage later determined that the man found wandering naked in Kahana was the same person seen in the footage from the resort, police said.

Maui Police Department did not publicly identify the suspect by name, citing a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruling and its policy against routinely releasing identifying information about people who have been arrested.

item.title: 'Fire Country' star Diane Farr reveals where she now lives after leaving Los Angeles behind
item.description: Diane Farr reveals she left Los Angeles after 30 years for rural Washington and plans to split time between Vancouver and Spain in her "third act."
item.content:encoded:
"Fire Country" star Diane Farr has revealed where she is now living after leaving Los Angeles behind.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, Farr explained that once her children went off to college, she didn't feel tied to California anymore and decided to put down roots in rural Washington. She also plans to split her time between Vancouver and Spain.

"So I actually moved to rural Washington because I could buy this pretty house, and it wasn't very expensive in comparison to living in LA for all those years," she said. "I live right on the water, so there's a lot of stand-up paddling and there's a lot of e-biking and really drinking in this gorgeous Pacific Northwest weather."

Farr stars in "Fire Country," which is filmed in Vancouver. Farr plays Sharon Leone on "Fire Country," a Cal Fire Division Chief and the mother of Bode Leone. 

"Fire Country" Season 5 is scheduled to premiere on October 9, 2026, airing Fridays at 9/8c on CBS and streaming the next day on Paramount+.

Farr told Fox News Digital that once her children went off to college and left California, she felt like she had "permission" to do the same.

'FIRE COUNTRY' STAR DIANE FARR LEAVES LOS ANGELES AFTER 30 YEARS TO START HER 'THIRD ACT'

"The permission came from my children being old enough that they live somewhere else. You know, they go to college, they live in other states, and I know women always talk about empty nest syndrome, and mine was unique," Farr began. "I didn't leave LA for 15 years when I had babies. I was afraid of working out of town. I was afraid of missing everything. I was afraid to do a one-hour drama."

WATCH: Diane Farr finds her joy in the Pacific Northwest

The actress explained that she had her children when she was nearly 40 and "really wanted to be there."

"After the pandemic, 15 years had gone by. We spent two years at home and everybody was a teenager and mean to mom. And I thought, I can leave, I could go to Vancouver. I'm taking that drama," she continued.

Farr said that her "third act" was focused around how she could get more joy out of her life.

"My third act is gonna look like six months of the year in Spain and six months of the year in Vancouver, because it's really like how to get the joie de vie. It's how to live the most," Farr said.

WATCH: 'Fire Country' star Diane Farr teases Sharon’s 'off the rails' era in Season 5

At the end of July, Farr shared with her Instagram followers that she was leaving Los Angeles after 30 years.

"I wasn’t born here, I didn’t go to school here — I just had a chance for representation as an actor and I moved out of NYC the summer I was 26," she wrote. "I came like most of the people I love in Hollywoodland — none of which I saw this week bc moving sucks."

'VAMPIRE DIARIES' STAR IAN SOMERHALDER SAYS LEAVING HOLLYWOOD FOR FARMING 'SHIFTED MY LIFE FOREVER'

She went on to say that she came to Los Angeles "chasing a dream that I am still shocked worked out."

Farr's acting career began in the '90s, with the actress landing her breakthrough role in "Roswell" in 1999. She later earned leading roles in "Numb3rs," "Splitting Up Together" and, most recently, "Fire Country."

In addition to her acting career, Farr also reflected on the many other positive experiences she had while living in Los Angeles, including starting a family.

"I also got to raise babies in the sun and the mountains and enjoy this beautiful home and attend public schools ??" she said. "Pinch me I’m overwhelmed by the blessings and hope, really hope I gave enough back. LA will always be where my family is from."

WATCH: 'Fire Country' star Diane Farr is choosing joy in her 'third act'

Farr shares three children with her ex-husband, Seung Yong Chung: son Beckett, 18, and twin daughters Coco and Sawyer, 17.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Farr explained what fans can expect from Sharon in season five.

"Well, last year was a lot of grief, right? Because she had lost Vince and this year she seems to have gotten some action with a very handsome man at the end of last season. So, I was sort of looking at it like Sharon hasn't dated or been single or been a party of one since she's about 20," she began. "So she's a little off the rails, you know, like she's kind of behaving like a 20-year-old. Which isn't good when you're the boss, and you have children and people responsible for you."

Farr concluded, "So, she's not making her best choices this season."

item.title: Grocery boss warns Mamdani's city-run stores pit government against 'its own citizens'
item.description: Gristedes CEO warns New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's $70 million city-run grocery stores will devastate bodegas and supermarkets nearby.
item.content:encoded:
As New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani moves ahead with a plan to open five city-run grocery stores, one of the Big Apple’s biggest supermarket owners has a blunt warning: the stores won't feed the hungry, but they will shelve the bodegas next door.

"The fact is the people [Mamdani] is going to hurt are the current bodegas or the current supermarkets in those neighborhoods," John Catsimatidis, CEO of the New York City grocery chain Gristedes, told Fox News Digital. "So it becomes a problem of ‘for whom do the bells toll?’"

In July, Mamdani announced the stores would be located in each of the city’s five boroughs, with the first location set to open in Hunts Point in the Bronx in late 2027. The mayor added he hopes to have all five stores operational before his term ends in 2030, and has set the project’s capital budget at an eye-watering $70 million.

MAMDANI’S CITY GROCERY PLAN COULD LEAVE TAXPAYERS PAYING FOR EVERY BANANA

The government-run shops will offer a 30% discount on a "core basket of everyday groceries," including meat, seafood and fresh produce, in an attempt to combat the affordability crisis plaguing the city, according to Mamdani’s administration.

"Every week, New Yorkers walk into a grocery store hoping the prices haven’t gone up again. A trip to the grocery store shouldn’t spell dread for New Yorkers," Mamdani said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani’s administration for comment.

The city is currently accepting applications from private operators interested in managing the logistical challenges of running the stores. Mamdani’s administration has also vowed to cover the property taxes and rental costs for each location — a decision that Catsimatidis feels puts local business owners at a disadvantage.

NY GOVERNOR HOPEFUL VOWS SHOWDOWN WITH MAMDANI OVER SOCIALIST AGENDA: ‘I WILL STOP HIM’

"The people that are going to run those five stores are not going to pay any real estate taxes. Not going to pay any rent," Catsimatidis said. "If I don’t pay any rent or real estate taxes, I can bring down the cost of a product 20% across the board."

In recent years, business owners throughout the five boroughs have been faced with expanding hurdles taking aim at their bottom line.

Catsimatidis added that local owners are already dealing with increased competition from outside vendors who rely on online commerce to reach consumers in the Big Apple, with the average grocery store operating at just a 1% to 3% profit margin.

GROCER-TURNED-LAWMAKER SAYS MAMDANI’S GOVERNMENT-RUN STORES 'MIGHT NOT EVEN LAST A YEAR'

"The businesses that are doing business outside New York City are just shipping [products] in by mail, they can afford to be cheaper," Catsimatidis said. "And you know what happens? They put the stores and the businesses inside New York City out of business."

According to the grocery tycoon, new and increasing costs — including congestion pricing and the rising cost of electricity — are also cutting business owners in New York City off at the knees.

"The big picture is that five stores in five boroughs is only good for public relations, and it's not really going to help the hungry," Catsimatidis told Fox News Digital. "Congestion pricing is hurting the stores in Manhattan a great deal. If you go up and down the streets in New York City, half the stores are empty — which is horrible."

Catsimatidis pointed out that Manhattan’s congestion pricing — which was enacted in January 2025 — puts a premium on deliveries traveling south of 61st Street.

"If I want stuff delivered to us from vendors in New Jersey — and all these companies are in New Jersey, Nassau, Suffolk County, Brooklyn, Queens or the Bronx — and I say to them, ‘I want you to deliver to New York City,' they're going to charge me 10% more, or 15% more," Catsimatidis said.

I WATCHED CHICAGO PROMISE FOOD EQUITY. NOW MY NEIGHBORHOOD HAS EMPTY SHELVES

While the solution to rolling out affordable grocery options without infringing on businesses within the area isn’t necessarily black and white, Catsimatidis is offering his own suggestion on how Mamdani’s administration can walk the line.

"If they’re not given credits to reduce their prices, then they’re going to be hurting," Catsimatidis said. "If you want me to lower the price of eggs, well maybe I’ll lower the price of the eggs by a dollar a dozen. But maybe [the city] will give me a dollar a dozen credit toward my real estate taxes."

"If you want to lower the prices for all Americans, all New Yorkers, well let’s do it right and lower it in all five boroughs," he added.

While Mamdani’s rollout of the city-run grocery stores has not come without critics, director of the CUNY Urban Food Policy Institute Nevin Cohen emphasized New York City’s dire need for officials to combat food insecurity among its residents.

THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE

"The problem is that many people can’t afford food for their families," Cohen told Fox News Digital. "1.4 million New Yorkers are food insecure, which means that they’re unsure whether they have enough money to put food on the table. Twenty percent of New Yorkers depend on SNAP benefits or federal food subsidies to put food on the table for the family."

Cohen also pointed to an existing program titled "FRESH," which aims to identify food deserts within New York City.

"It provides tax incentives and zoning incentives to encourage new supermarkets or the expansion of existing supermarkets in neighborhoods deemed to be underserved by food retail," Cohen said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

While Catsimatidis agrees the city-run grocery stores are being placed in neighborhoods throughout the city that would serve lower-income residents, he remains worried about the impact the shops will have on businesses in the immediate area, while pointing to Mamdani’s democratic socialist platform.

"You're competing against your own citizens, and that's only done in socialist countries," Catsimatidis told Fox News Digital. "Look at socialist countries — nobody's breaking down the walls to get in, but they're all breaking down the walls to get into the United States of America."

item.title: New power axis in the making? Three military heavyweights lock arms, complicating Abraham Accords strategy
item.description: The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan raises questions about whether it signals a Middle East shift from the U.S.
item.content:encoded:
A new defense pact linking Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan is fueling debate over whether the three countries are laying the groundwork for a competing regional bloc — potentially challenging the U.S.-backed architecture built around Israel and the Abraham Accords — or simply creating a new model of burden-sharing among American partners.

The three countries, all with longstanding security ties to the United States, enter the pact with different interests — but together they could begin shifting the region’s balance of power.

Saudi Arabia signed a Strategic Defense Agreement with the United States in November 2025 and was designated a major non-NATO ally, but Riyadh did not secure the treaty-level, Article 5-style U.S. defense guarantee it had long sought, making the new pact a potential hedge against uncertainty over Washington’s future security commitments.

 Pakistan, a nuclear-armed state, gains greater energy security, Saudi investment and regional influence, while offering significant military capabilities — although whether its nuclear deterrent extends to its partners remains unconfirmed. Turkey, already a NATO member, gains a larger market for its growing defense industry and additional strategic weight as tensions with Israel rise.

WHO IS TURKEY'S RECEP TAYYIP ERDOĞAN? HOW NATO'S MOST UNPREDICTABLE LEADER KEEPS REINVENTING HIMSELF

Taken together, the arrangement gives three U.S. partners greater ability to build deterrence on their own — potentially easing Washington’s security burden while also giving them more independence from it.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on Aug. 7. A joint statement said the pact was intended to "strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression" and stipulated that an armed attack against one country would be regarded as an attack against all three.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan went further the following day, telling Turkey’s state-run Anadolu news agency that the agreement was "technically the same" as NATO’s Article 5 mutual-defense provision, which treats an attack on one member as an attack on all. Fidan said, however, that the countries would consult on the degree and form of assistance provided following an attack, with operational details still to be determined by a new ministerial committee. The alliance will also establish a general secretariat based in Saudi Arabia, Reuters reported Aug. 8.

Fidan said President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan wants the alliance to eventually expand beyond its three founding members and identified Egypt as a potential participant. He said negotiations over the pact had been underway for two years and eight months.

Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly has pushed back on suggestions that the agreement represents the creation of a new sectarian or military bloc, saying it is not connected to nuclear ambitions or an arms race. Turkish officials have similarly said the pact is defensive and not directed against Iran or any other country.

Iran, meanwhile, played down the pact as a threat to Tehran. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Aug. 10 that Iran saw no reason to be concerned that the agreement was directed against it, telling Reuters that the pact reflected a regional shift toward countries relying more heavily on their own security capabilities rather than outside powers.

"Any plan that is based on the geopolitical and historical realities of the region, is comprehensive and inclusive, and correctly identifies the enemy and the threat, has a chance of helping to strengthen security and prevent instability and abuses by the Zionist enemy and its allies," Baghaei said, referring to Israel.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Turkish Embassy in Washington, D.C., and the Pakistani government for comment but did not receive responses in time for publication.

Sinan Ciddi, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies and director of its Turkey program, told Fox News Digital that he remains skeptical that the pact currently amounts to a NATO-style alliance.

AMERICANS ARE NOT GIVING UP ON NATO, BUT THEY EXPECT EUROPE TO DO ITS SHARE

"Does it have teeth? Is it a serious deterrent? Is that a serious collective defense pact? Is it a Muslim NATO? We're not actually sure yet," Ciddi said.

Ciddi said each of the three countries enters the pact with different incentives. For Saudi Arabia, he sees it as a hedge against doubts over the reliability of U.S. security guarantees; for Pakistan, it offers greater energy security, Saudi investment and added regional prestige; and for Turkey, it creates new opportunities for defense cooperation and a larger market for its arms industry. Ankara also gains additional deterrent weight as its tensions with Israel grow, he argued.

"I would say that this pact is much more targeted towards closer economic and commercial ties rather than substantive NATO-like security ties," Ciddi added.

Saudi Arabia rejects the suggestion that the agreement represents a turn away from Washington.

WATCH: DEMOCRATS BLAST TRUMP SAUDI NUCLEAR DEAL AS GOP TOUTS REGIONAL ALLIANCE

"The United States remains to be our primary strategic partner," a Saudi source told Fox News Digital on background, saying the kingdom’s expanding ties with Pakistan and Turkey should not be viewed as coming at the expense of its relationship with Washington.

The Saudi source also rejected descriptions of the agreement as a "Muslim NATO" or Sunni alliance and said it was not directed against Israel, Iran or any other particular country. Asked whether the pact represented a Saudi move away from normalization with Israel, the source said, "It's not related in any way."

Aziz Alghashian, a senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, offered a similar interpretation.

"I don't think it's a counterweight to the Abraham Accords," Alghashian told Fox News Digital.

WHY NATO’S DEFENSE SPENDING IMBALANCE LASTED FOR DECADES

Instead, Alghashian described the agreement as part of Saudi Arabia’s longer-term diversification of strategic relationships.

"I think it's actually a supplementation. It's complementary to the United States," he said, arguing that greater cooperation among regional partners could provide increased burden-sharing for Washington.

From Pakistan’s perspective, the agreement offers both military and political advantages, Raza Rumi, distinguished lecturer at the Roosevelt House Public Policy Institute at CUNY, told Fox News Digital.

"Pakistan gains strategic depth, greater leverage in the Gulf and a more formal place in an emerging regional security architecture," Rumi said, pointing to potential cooperation on defense production, technology transfers, intelligence, training and air and missile defense.

But he cautioned against interpreting the pact’s mutual-defense language too literally.

"Seriously, but not literally as an Article 5-style guarantee, at least not yet," Rumi said. Its credibility, he added, will depend on whether the countries develop joint planning, command structures and procedures for responding to crises.

Rumi also warned against assuming the Middle East is already dividing into two fixed camps. India, however, is watching the new alignment closely. India’s Ministry of External Affairs said Aug. 11 that it was examining the pact’s implications for national security and regional peace and stability, adding that New Delhi would take "whatever necessary steps are required" to safeguard its interests.

"These states are hedging, not choosing permanent blocs," he said.

TRUMP SQUEEZED BETWEEN ISRAEL AND TURKEY AS NETANYAHU, ERDOGAN ESCALATE FEUD

Ciddi, on the other hand, argued that the agreement reflects "serious reservations" among regional countries about U.S. security guarantees. His greater concern is that even a militarily weak pact could encourage opposing alignments to harden.

"Security pacts beget more security pacts," Ciddi said, arguing that Israel, Greece, Cyprus and potentially India could deepen their own cooperation in response.

"You're buying security, but you're also creating tension," he said. "That's where I think the harm comes in."

Calling the pact a direct counterweight to the Abraham Accords or the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor would therefore be "premature," Rumi argued. But he said a broader competition is emerging over the region’s future — between U.S.-backed economic integration involving India, Israel and the Gulf and efforts by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to develop greater strategic autonomy.

item.content:encoded:
Golf: the only sport in which the fans care more about the regular season than the playoffs. In fact, most of you thought the PGA TOUR 2026 season ended after the final major, the British Open. But, nope. The FedExCup Playoffs start this week with the FedEx St. Jude Championship at TPC Southwind in Memphis, Tennessee.

Only the top 69 golfers in the FedExCup standings head to Memphis for the first round of the playoffs because Daniel Berger withdrew. With no cut and massive playoff points at stake, only the top 50 in the standings advance to next week's BMW Championship.

PAR TALK: INCREDIBLE MICHAEL BLOCK DRAMA, YOUNG AMERICAN STREAK CONTINUES ON PGA TOUR AND JOAQUIN NIEMANN DOES IT AGAIN

TPC Southwind is a 7,288-yard, par-70 that rewards precise iron play more than mindless bombing. Water is in play throughout; the Bermuda greens can get tricky, and missed approaches bring bogey into the equation quickly. Hence, I'm upweighting ball-striking and course management in my handicap.

My betting strategy for the St. Jude Championship is to wager enough on a golfer's outright to profit 20 units (u), while backing them up with top-10 and 20 bets. That said, let's talk about the guys I'm backing in the first round of the FedExCup Playoffs.

2026 FedEx St. Jude Championship Best Bets

The following odds are from when I bet on the golfers listed below. Subject to change.

🇯🇵 Hideki Matsuyama +3300 (0.61u) at DraftKings and Top-10 with ties +240 (0.5u) at Kalshi

🇳🇴 Viktor Hovland +4356 (0.46u) at Kalshi and Top-10 with ties +275 (0.5u) at BetMGM

🇺🇸 Justin Thomas +5146 (0.39u) at Polymarket and Top-10 with ties +275 (0.5u) at BetMGM

🇰🇷 Tom Kim +5500 (0.36u) at DraftKings and Top-20 with ties +146 (0.75u) at Kalshi

🇺🇸 Rickie Fowler +8481 (0.24u) at Polymarket and Top-20 with ties +189 (0.75u) at Kalshi

‘Deki has five straight T20-or-better finishes at TPC Southwind, and I cashed on him when he won the 2024 St. Jude Championship at +3000. Furthermore, he has the best course history in this field, according to Betsperts Golf’s Ron Klos.

Matsuyama has five consecutive T14-or-better finishes entering the 2026 St. Jude, with a T3 (3M Open), T5 (Rocket Classic) and T7 (Wyndham Championship) in his last three tournaments.

Hideki has gained strokes on the field in driving accuracy in six consecutive starts, has picked up strokes putting in four of his last five outings, has a world-class short-game and is dialed in with his irons.

Between his skill set and the course history/fit, Matsuyama should have a shorter price than many names ahead of him on the betting board, so I’m taking the value.

I’m probably missing something, but Hovland shouldn’t have worse odds here than Patrick Cantlay and Si Woo Kim, who haven’t won this season, or in the last couple of seasons for that matter.

Hovland won the 2026 Travelers Championship at another TPC course (River Highlands) three starts back and nearly won the 2024 St. Jude by finishing T2.

Iron play is a separator at TPC Southwind, and Hovland has gained strokes on approach in all four majors this year and eight straight starts. Viktor is a notoriously crappy chipper, but around-the-green is deemphasized at TPC Southwind.

Regardless, as long as he plays his game this weekend — dialed in with his irons and accurate off-the-tee — Hovland will be in the mix on Sunday.

Okay, so JT is down to +3605 at Polymarket now, and I'm sorry. But I gave out my full betting card for the St. Jude via X/Twitter Monday, and I've only hit one outright this season. Meaning, if you don't want to bet Thomas at the current odds, it's a good thing you didn't see it on X.

Also, I'm not even sure why JT's number has come down so far. I know why I bet him, and I'll get into that in a second. However, DataGolf.com, which is like scripture in the golf betting community, makes his true odds +2975. Bookmaker, the sharpest sportsbook for golf, has Thomas at +3002 as of Wednesday at midnight.

Back to why I bet JT. He's won the 2020 St. Jude Invitational, and a couple of his 14 other PGA TOUR wins have come at similar courses with a ton of water hazards, such as TPC Sawgrass (THE 2021 PLAYERS Championship) and PGA National (The 2018 Honda Classic).

Thomas gained strokes on approach in his six visits to TPC Southwind. His biggest weakness is driving accuracy, and he hit a higher rate of fairways than the field in nine of his last 10 starts, including four straight, per DataGolf.com.

JT has played well this season — eight top-20 finishes, highlighted by a T4 at the 2026 PGA Championship — and if he can stay out of the water, he should play much better this week than his odds indicate.

The South Korean cashed a big top-20 bet for me last week by tying for fifth at the Wyndham Championship, so I'm happy to reinvest that money back into him this week. Kim won the 2026 Genesis Scottish Open four starts back, two weeks after nearly winning the U.S. Open, where he finished third.

More importantly, his game is a perfect fit for this course. Because of all the water, accuracy off-the-tee and with your irons is important at TPC Southwind, and Kim is one of the most precise ball-strikers in the world. He ranks second in this field for Strokes Gained (SG): Approach over the last 40 rounds, per Bet The Number.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Kim has gained strokes with his irons and in driving accuracy in all three St. Judes from 2022-24. He's picked up strokes on approach in 15 of his last 16 starts, including 11 straight, according to DataGolf.com. Yeah, it's unlikely he'll win again in a short span, but Kim's fair odds are roughly +4000.

Fowler has had a roller coaster season, but he comes into the St. Jude with strong lead-in form. He has 10 top-20 finishes in 19 events this season, including three straight: T15 at the John Deere Classic, T18 at the British Open and T8 at the Rocket Classic.

At last year's St. Jude, Fowler ranked fifth in SG: Ball-striking (driving and approach) in a T6 finish, per Betsperts Golf, and he was playing worse last season. item.title: Accused Charlie Kirk assassin Tyler Robinson asks judge to take potential death penalty off table
item.description: Tyler Robinson's defense argues prosecutors failed to prove the sole aggravating factor that could make Charlie Kirk's killing a death penalty case.
item.content:encoded:
Lawyers for accused Charlie Kirk assassin Tyler Robinson are arguing that prosecutors haven't established a case for the potential death penalty in a new court filing made public Tuesday night.

"The facts and the law require this Court to strike the sole aggravating factor," defense attorneys Kathy Nester, Michael Burt, Richard Novak and Staci Visser wrote in a 41-page brief.

After a weeklong preliminary hearing in early July, Judge Tony Graf Jr. gave both sides in the case time to file briefs before he makes a decision on whether there is enough probable cause to send the case to trial — which he is expected to announce on Sept. 1.

CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION

Robinson, 23, is accused of shooting the 31-year-old Kirk at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025, during a Turning Point USA event. Kirk had founded the group to promote conservatism on campuses around the country and was speaking in front of a crowd of more than 2,000 in the courtyard when he was struck and killed by a single bullet.

Robinson's defense argued in Tuesday's filing that prosecutors didn't establish probable cause concerning the aggravating factor — that the shooting created a high probability of death to someone other than Kirk and that Robinson knew of that "high probability."

SEND US A TIP

Without the aggravator, the potential death penalty would be taken off the table.

"The State had over ten months to investigate the shooting death of Charlie Kirk and to develop legally sufficient evidence that Mr. Robinson 'knowingly created a great risk of death to another other than Charlie Kirk and the defendant,' the sole aggravator alleged in the Information which in theory exposes Mr. Robinson to the potential punishment of death," Robinson's attorneys wrote. "The State’s presentation of its evidence as to this alleged circumstance in aggravation at the preliminary hearing in July 2026 wholly fails to carry its burden of proof."

FRIEND OF CHARLIE KIRK LABELS COURTROOM EVIDENCE 'DEVASTATING' AFTER CHILLING SURVEILLANCE FOOTAGE SHOWN

Robinson's lawyers noted that there was only one shot fired and that it struck Kirk. No one else was hit.

They also argued that no one else was in the line of fire — noting that the bullet came from the rooftop, following a downward trajectory before striking Kirk.

"The only evidence presented supports that the bullet travelled above, not through, the crowd," they wrote.

TYLER ROBINSON'S AND LANCE TWIGGS' DNA BOTH ALLEGEDLY FOUND ON KEY EVIDENCE IN CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION

When the suspected murder weapon was recovered, a .30-06 bolt-action Mauser rifle, there was a spent casing in the chamber and three unfired rounds.

And the evidence introduced by Utah County prosecutors indicates Kirk was the lone target, according to the defense filing.

TYLER ROBINSON'S DEFENSE SUFFERS DUAL SETBACKS AS JUDGE HOLDS OFF ON DEATH PENALTY DECISION

"The communications the State admitted between Mr. Robinson and Mr. Twiggs indicate Mr. Robinson’s intention to kill Charlie Kirk," the defense wrote, citing an alleged message from Robinson: "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk and I took it."

"There is no mention of any threat or intended harm to any other individual(s)."

Prosecutors have a deadline next week to reply to the brief. Graf's decision is expected at the Sept. 1 hearing.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Donna Rotunno, a Chicago-based lawyer and Fox News contributor, said Robinson's argument is a long-shot, especially at the probable cause stage of the case.

"The evidence in the preliminary hearing has already proven that there were many people there," she told Fox News Digital Wednesday. "The evidence has shown where the shooter was vs. where Charlie was and where the shot was taken from, the amount of people who were in the line of fire. They can argue those facts from other pieces of evidence that they've introduced. They didn’t need somebody specifically to get on the witness stand and say there were all these people in danger."

Prosecutors have alleged that Robinson is the man who appears on surveillance video approaching a sniper's perch. According to investigators, the killer opened fire from a rooftop on the far side of the packed courtyard, which was full of spectators.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"If you drive a car into a crowd, that whole crowd is in danger," Rotunno added. "I don’t think that argument is a stretch."

TYLER ROBINSON ASKS FOR MORE SECRET HEARINGS AFTER LOSING FIGHT OVER CAMERAS IN COURT

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Robinson's lawyers also renewed their attempt to throw out hearsay evidence from the preliminary hearing, arguing that prosecutors haven't established its reliability.

Similar objections failed in July, and Rotunno said she expects them to fail again.

"They're relitigating many issues that the judge has already ruled on, and they're going nowhere," she said.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

The defense is also asking Graf to strike two lesser charges — witness tampering and committing a violent offense in the presence of a child — arguing that Robinson was advising his roommate Lance Twiggs to exercise his constitutional rights and that prosecutors failed to show Robinson knew children were present at the time of the shooting.

UTAH VALLEY UNIVERSITY SCRAPS CONTROVERSIAL COMMENCEMENT SPEAKER WHO CRITICIZED CHARLIE KIRK AFTER HIS MURDER

And they argue that the enhancement that Kirk was targeted for his political expression should also be dropped, disputing an alleged text from Robinson to Twiggs stating, "I had enough of his hatred."

"It is the State that argues that because Mr. Robinson and Mr. Twiggs are two men who love each other and/or, it speculates, because Mr. Twiggs (and not Mr. Robinson) was at least intermittently identifying as a female to his close friends, it is Mr. Kirk’s views on these topics which are the 'hatred' Mr. Robinson was referring to," the defense wrote. "These circumstances are not sufficient to establish, even by probable cause which if any political expression of Mr. Kirk motivated Mr. Robinson to select Mr. Kirk for an act of violence."

Robinson has not yet entered a plea.

item.title: Blakeman cuts into Hochul's New York governor's race lead in new poll, as likely voters give DSA judgment
item.description: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s lead over Bruce Blakeman narrowed from 20 points among registered voters in Siena’s June poll to 10 points among likely voters in its latest poll.
item.content:encoded:
New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul’s lead over Republican candidate Bruce Blakeman is slipping, according to a new Siena University poll released Wednesday, as likely voters in New York also gave a negative 30-47% favorability rating to the Democratic Socialists of America.

With under three months to go until Election Day, Hochul leads Blakeman 49-39% among likely New York State gubernatorial voters, down from 52-32% when registered voters were asked the same question in June.

"At this point four years ago, August 2022, when Hochul was just finishing her first year as governor, she led her opponent, former Republican Congressman (and current EPA Administrator) Lee Zeldin by 14 points, 53-39%, before going on to ultimately win the election by six points, 53-47%," Siena pollster Steven Greenberg said in a statement.

Blakeman, who is the current Nassau County executive, said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Wednesday that "All of the polls we have seen in the last two months have us virtually tied with Kathy Hochul," and, "This poll is always off and continues to be off."

HOCHUL SAYS STEFANIK WOULD'VE BEEN TOUGHER GOP OPPONENT THAN BLAKEMAN IN SURPRISING SWIPE AT RIVAL

"We know and she knows this race is neck and neck. Kathy Hochul is desperate for people to believe that she is way ahead when she knows that her high taxes, soaring electric bills, and increased crime have made her the worst governor in America," Blakeman added.

The latest Siena University Poll was conducted between Aug. 3–6 among 811 New York likely voters, with an overall margin of error of +/- 4.6 percentage points for those who answered the entire survey.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Hochul’s campaign for comment.

The Siena poll found that likely voters believe Hochul will do a better job than Blakeman on making prices more affordable for average New Yorkers, 48–41%, and increasing the supply of affordable housing, 51–35%.

NEW YORK SHERIFFS 'MAD AS HELL' AS HOCHUL PUSHES TO BAN KEY LAW ENFORCEMENT PARTNERSHIP

Respondents were more divided over the issues of keeping New Yorkers safe, where Hochul led 47-44%, and addressing undocumented immigrants living in the state, where she was ahead 45-44%, according to the Siena Research Institute.

"Not surprisingly, both candidates are holding on to their partisan bases, as Hochul leads among Democrats 80-8% and Blakeman leads among Republicans 84-9%. Likely independent voters favor Blakeman by a narrow five-point margin, 45–40%," Greenberg said.

"Hochul holds a commanding 64-19% lead in New York City, but trails Blakeman in the downstate suburbs by eight points, 49-41%. They are running virtually even in upstate, as well as among men and with white voters; Hochul has large leads with women, Latinos and Black voters," he added.

The Siena Research Institute also said it asked voters about the Democratic Socialists of America for the first time. The progressive political group has been exerting its influence on elections across America, with member Zohran Mamdani winning the New York City mayoral race last year.

The poll found that the group had a negative favorability rating.

"Democrats view the DSA favorably, 50–21%, while 82% of Republicans and 57% of independents have an unfavorable view of the DSA," the Siena Research Institute said.

Fox News Digital's Danielle Wallace contributed to this report.

item.title: Iran-backed Houthi threat in Red Sea could lead to major US policy shift, analysts say
item.description: Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping may push the U.S. to forge closer ties with Somaliland, analysts say, as concerns grow over Djibouti's reliability and China's expanding presence.
item.content:encoded:
JOHANNESBURG: As the Iran-backed Houthis step up their threat to Red Sea shipping, analysts say the U.S. could consider a major change in strategy.

Houthi attacks on ships passing through a vital chokepoint may lead Washington to cement relations with more reliable partners along Africa’s coastline.

Somaliland is a pro-U.S. outpost, having broken away from war-torn Somalia in 1991, and is offering the U.S. the use of one of the longest runways in Africa, an air base and a deep sea port on the Red Sea.

IRAN AND HOUTHI TERROR PROXY FACING RED SEA THREAT FROM PRO-US AFRICAN NATION

The Houthis have vowed to close the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, a narrow waterway through which Saudi Arabia exports up to 7 million barrels of oil a day, now that access to the Strait of Hormuz is severely restricted. In the past month in the Red Sea, the Houthis have reportedly attacked Saudi-flagged ships, are said to have sunk an Indian commercial cargo vessel and, on Aug. 13, an Egyptian cargo ship was hit, with at least four of its crew killed.

The U.S. already has a large military base on the Red Sea in Djibouti, but this is claimed to be increasingly problematic. "China is significantly expanding its military and commercial presence in Djibouti," Edmund Fitton-Brown previously told Fox News Digital.

Fitton-Brown, the former British ambassador to the Houthis’ home country, Yemen, and a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, (FDD), added, "There is a sense that Djibouti is not a reliable ally for the U.S. So Somaliland’s time has probably come."

Major General Ken Ekman, who retired last year from being the Department of War’s West Africa Coordination Element Lead, said, in essence, the Houthis could force the U.S. into recognizing Somaliland as an independent state. "The Houthis could compel a different U.S. strategy in Africa."

TRUMP THREATENS 'MAJOR MILITARY PUNISHMENT' FOR IRAN OVER FUTURE HOUTHI ATTACKS

Ekman said the Houthis are building up a second front in this Middle East conflict. "It distracts the U.S. and stretches our assets," he added.

"The Houthis have a strategy of their own. They are testing U.S. military ability, and are likely to pull the trigger in a major way when Iranian influence in the Strait of Hormuz wanes in leverage."

He said that recently the U.S. Africa Command, AFRICOM, has concentrated on looking at land-based threats. "To date, our Africa strategy is driven by counterterrorism missions against Islamist al Qaeda and ISIS-linked groups based in Africa."

He continued, "These groups pose a limited and not immediate threat to the U.S. homeland. Overall, Red Sea basing to date has focused more on crisis response in East Africa, countering and competing against Russia and China."

COULD THIS AFRICAN NATION BECOME TRUMP'S NEXT TERROR TARGET AS JIHADISTS CLOSE IN ON POWER?

Ekman added, "orienting a Horn of Africa strategy against the Houthis would place a premium on freedom of navigation. Somaliland is proximate and overcomes some of the limitations imposed by other regional hosts like Djibouti and Middle East partners."

Limitations and an apparent sense of frustration with Somalia, Somaliland’s neighbor and rival, have been expressed in a warning from U.S. Air Force Gen. Dagvin Anderson, commander of U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM).

In a recent interview with a Somali journalist, he was asked whether the U.S. was pulling out of the nation and turning its back on it.

Anderson said the U.S. has not turned its back on Somalia, having been committed to the country for several years, he noted the success of its counterterrorism group known as DANAB, which he said is "one of the most capable forces on the continent." He noted that "it was up to Somalia to sustain that force… to build it and continue to make it effective going into the future and use it as it was designed to counter terrorism."

Referring to the Somali government’s apparent lack of ability to deal decisively with Islamist al-Shabab terrorists, Anderson seemingly hinted at pulling some or even all military support. "If Somalia steps up and the government steps up and takes the lead on this, we will continue to be there because there is mutual interest."

He continued, "But if we can’t see that in, the political instability and political infighting continues, then it’s going to be very hard for us to continue to stay engaged."

Bill Roggio, editor of the Long War Journal, said Washington is fed up with Mogadishu, but currently not enough for the U.S. to change allegiance to Somaliland.

He told Fox News Digital, "The U.S. has expressed displeasure with the Somali government's rampant corruption and internal infighting with local and regional governments, and with various clans. However, full recognition of Somaliland independence would create a major rift between the U.S. and Somalia."

Roggio didn’t rule out the U.S. operating a second Red Sea base in Somaliland, saying "U.S. forces situated at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti are far better situated geographically to deter the Houthis from shutting down the Bab el Mandeb Strait than a potential base in Somaliland. That being said, redundancy (back up plan) is a good thing in military operations."

"The United States needs reliable partners on Africa's coastline," Bashir Goth, Somaliland Representative to the United States, told Fox News Digital.

Goth said, "Somaliland is that partner and our defense officials have been in active dialogue with AFRICOM on Red Sea security. Somaliland has the geography, the stability and the will to work closely with Washington — and will continue to do so."

TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR

Officially, the U.S. still stands with Somalia, in preference to Somaliland.

item.title: Former MLB star calls for salary fix as owners, Players Association talk 'two different languages'
item.description: Nick Swisher warns MLB's collective bargaining negotiation could derail the sport's attendance boom if owners and the Players Association can't agree.
item.content:encoded:
The current collective bargaining agreement between Major League Baseball and the Players' Association expires in roughly three and a half months, and there seems to be no resolution in sight.

Players are adamant that they will not play under a salary cap, which has been formally proposed by owners for the first time since 1994 — and we all know how that worked out.

"It really does feel like the players' union and the commissioner's office are speaking two different languages right now," former MLB star Nick Swisher said in a recent interview with Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

It's horrible timing for the game amid a recent boom, as attendance has increased for three consecutive years for the first time since it did each year from 2004 to 2007. In 1995, after a players' strike that cost the '94 postseason, attendance was grim at MLB ballparks.

Swisher, though, has been on both sides of the coin — he won a World Series with the New York Yankees in 2009 and now has a role in their front office as well as the league itself. So, he has advice for both sides.

"I think just in general, the players have a lot of things that they can give, and I think the commissioner's office has some things that they can give, too. So, I think one of the things that I've always realized, especially now being in the business world, is you can't go into a negotiation trying to win. That always ends up bad," he said.

"I'm interested to see how these negotiations are going to come. Are we trying to come to an agreement or are we trying to win the negotiation? So, regardless if it's [MLBPA interim executive director] Bruce Meyer, if it's Rob Manfred in the commissioner's office, I just want the boys to figure it out. Man, we're in such a great spot right now. We need to continue to keep this game going because I don't want it to stop, because when it stops, the fans, they get angry about that. All of a sudden, the money starts coming into play and then people don't support us as much anymore. We just need to continue to keep pushing forward and try and figure out how to make this happen because come 2027, baby, in April, I want to start that season off right."

Players will place blame on small-market teams for not spending money. Those small-market owners, however, will claim they cannot afford big contracts, leaving the superstars to the Los Angeles Dodgers, New York Mets, Yankees, and a small handful of others. But rather than a cap, Swisher wants to see a salary floor.

BLUE JAYS-RED SOX GAME THROWN INTO CHAOS BY 17-MINUTE 'RULES CHECK,' MASSIVE SCOREBOARD MISTAKE

"You can't have teams paying $60 million a year, because statistically, it shows that those low-market teams don't make it very far into the playoffs. That's just statistics. But I think just in general, if you all of a sudden start bringing that floor into play and then all of a sudden the 22nd, 23rd, 24th, 25th guy on the roster is all of a sudden making some good money, I think that both sides have some things to give and take, and I hope that it works itself out," Swisher said.

"We're in a good spot right now. The game is really, really great. Whether you want to blame the commissioner's office, whether you want to blame the Players' Association, either way, bro, for me, man, I just want to get it done. Get it done. I don't care who's at fault. I don't care who bets against what. Let's just find a way to get our boys back on the field next year."

Swisher was back on two fields this past weekend — after attending the Yankees' Old Timers' Day in the Bronx, he was in Central Park on behalf of Angry Orchard to surprise one of the worst recreational adult softball teams in the country and play for them to hopefully get a win (they did with the 2010 All-Star).

"To be part of something absolutely new and untraditional, to not only invest in the winners but to invest in the underdogs, bro. They say, don't get angry, get orchard," Swisher said. "Just being able to be part of this and to play with the Sons of Pitches today was absolutely legendary and an epic, man.

"To be able to team up with an organization in a company like Angry Orchard who stands for the right things and wants to invest in everybody. The inclusivity of all of this is something I really enjoy, and to be able to not only handle the winners of the world but to be able to invest in the underdogs too, I think is great. So, for me to be part of the underdogs today, to pull off a W, it was legendary."

item.title: NCAA has no plans to surrender, as eligibility lawsuits for 2022 class turn into an all-out legal war
item.description: The NCAA announced it will not grant a blanket waiver for the 2022 class, vowing to fight lawsuits over its age-based eligibility rule in court.
item.content:encoded:
During one of the most chaotic periods college athletics has seen when it comes to athlete eligibility, the NCAA made one thing clear Tuesday night: It has no plans to stop fighting the wave of lawsuits coming its way.

Right now, in courtrooms across the country, athletes who were part of the 2022 class are suing the NCAA over what they feel is a misguided and illegal decision that is preventing them from participating this academic year.

When the NCAA adopted its new age-based eligibility model, giving athletes five years to play five seasons, it made one critical decision that is currently being argued on a daily basis: it excluded the 2022 recruiting class from the new rule.

NCAA ROCKED BY COLORADO JUDGE'S 2022 CLASS ELIGIBILITY RULING THAT COULD RESHAPE COLLEGE SPORTS THIS YEAR

Athletes who believe they are being denied an extra season of competition began filing civil lawsuits in courtrooms from Colorado to South Carolina, arguing they should receive the same benefits as those covered under the new eligibility structure.

Now, the NCAA might simply be too deep into this fight to let go of the rope.

Or, perhaps more importantly, the organization understands what could happen if it grants a blanket waiver to every member of the 2022 class who would otherwise have another season of eligibility remaining under the new guidelines if grandfathered in.

Outside courtrooms, some athletic administrators have hinted to Fox News Digital-OutKick that the NCAA's thinking on not granting a blanket waiver or including the 2022 class could center around the fact that there are too many players and not enough roster spots across the country for this to work.

Right now, thanks to an injunction granted by U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney of Colorado, athletes from the class of 2022 were granted the ability to join rosters, provided there was a spot available.

That ruling has already led numerous football and basketball programs to add players who had another year of eligibility under Sweeney's order.

But the NCAA quickly responded, filing an emergency motion for a stay with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, which it mentioned in their hard stance on Tuesday night.

"The Tenth Circuit has ordered an expedited briefing on our request for a stay pending appeal," the NCAA noted about the appeal. The deadline for the class members to file a response to the emergency motion is Friday, August 14.  The NCAA's reply brief must be filed no later than Monday, August 17.  In the meantime, the Wisne injunction remains in effect."

That still left one major question hanging over college athletics: Would the NCAA eventually give in to the pressure and grant a blanket waiver rather than continue fighting lawsuits that have already been filed — and the additional ones still to come?

On Tuesday night, the NCAA delivered its answer.

It's not tapping out.

"The Division I Cabinet, including its student-athlete members, carefully considered whether to make the age-based eligibility rule apply retroactively, and decided that doing so would not be in the best interest of all current and future college athletes," the NCAA announced. "We stand behind and will continue to fully defend the membership's decision.  The injunction should never have been granted, and we have asked the Tenth Circuit to permanently reverse it."

INDIANA TAKES FULL ADVANTAGE OF NCAA COURTROOM CHAOS WITH STUNNING ROSTER MOVE AMID ELIGIBILITY FIGHT

And beyond the potentially massive ramifications of the Tenth Circuit's eventual decision, confusion remains over another important issue: Which athletes are allowed to enter the transfer portal?

On Tuesday night, attorney Ryan Downton noted to Fox News Digital-OutKick that a vast number of coaches he has spoken with during this process are siding with the athletes.

"The NCAA keeps calling it "the Membership’s decision" to exclude the Class of 2022," Downton noted. "But neither the NCAA schools nor the coaches got to vote on this proposal. The overwhelming majority of coaches I talk with want these kids to have a chance to play."

In states such as Tennessee and Ohio, injunctions granted in separate cases allow players who are plaintiffs in those lawsuits to use the transfer portal.

But in the Colorado case that athletic departments across the country are closely watching, the plaintiffs have not been granted an additional portal window.

The opinion of some is that the organization knew that implementing its new eligibility rule in June — rather than before the last portal window for each sport — could trigger a wave of lawsuits from athletes who suddenly found themselves on the wrong side of the new guidelines.

The roots of the current fight can be traced back to the Diego Pavia case and, maybe more importantly in the future, former Vanderbilt linebacker Langston Patterson's lawsuit against the NCAA in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee.

Patterson is currently challenging the NCAA over the number of years athletes are allowed to participate in college athletics.

And the concept behind the NCAA's new "age-based eligibility" rule had already been presented in court.

Attorney Ryan Downton, who represents Patterson and athletes in more recent lawsuits filed after the NCAA implemented its new eligibility rule, previously argued for what became known as the "five-for-five" model.

"We asked the NCAA to give everyone five years last year when we filed the Patterson lawsuit. They said no," Downton told Fox News Digital-OutKick last week.

"Now they’ve done it, but excluded the athletes asking for the change. It feels like the NCAA is saying, ‘you had a good idea, but we can’t let you enjoy the benefits of it.’ Just like they changed the name. We called it ‘five-for-five.’ They call it ‘age-based eligibility.’ It’s the same thing, but the NCAA tries to pretend it isn’t."

That's the part of this fight that will continue to fuel frustration among members of the 2022 class.

They wanted five years to play five seasons. The NCAA ultimately adopted a system that does essentially that. But the athletes who were already pushing for the change were left out.

Now, the NCAA has drawn a line in the sand and appears prepared to defend its stance across multiple states, with its most recent loss coming on Tuesday in a Texas courtroom.

Maybe the organization believes that refusing to make the rule retroactive is genuinely the right thing to do.

Or maybe NCAA officials understand they have little choice, given the potential fallout that could come with granting a blanket waiver and opening thousands of additional roster spots that don't actually exist.

Either way, the NCAA isn't waving the white flag.

And now, we wait on an appeals court in Colorado to deliver what will ultimately be a monumental decision.

item.title: Three school safety steps every parent should know before classes begin
item.description: A parent outlines three essential back-to-school safety steps, from demanding emergency training for educators to evaluating personal safety tools.
item.content:encoded:
I reviewed my children’s back-to-school shopping lists last week. After wrapping my head around the dizzying array of required items, I was struck by what was missing: safety.

Across America, parents will spend the next few weeks buying everything from notebooks, pens, and pencils to dorm fridges, shower caddies, and laundry baskets.

No parent wants their child to be "that kid" — the one who accidentally shows up on the first day with the wrong calculator or without gym shoes. Yet whether dropping them off at the bus stop or at the quad, almost none of them will send them away with an honest, practical conversation about safety — the one thing they need most.

IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT?

Why? Sometimes, because we assume our kids already know what to do or that someone else will teach them. Mostly because it’s uncomfortable. It’s easier to talk about spiral notebooks and extra-long twin sheets than about what to do if the unthinkable happens. But silence has not made our schools safer — and it has not made our children more prepared.

Real back-to-school readiness means facing potential threats head-on. As parents gear up for the school year, there are three essential steps they should take.

1. Demand that educators be trained and equipped for an emergency.

Teachers and other school staff are often the first line of defense in a crisis. That’s an enormous responsibility for people whose emergency training is often little more than a checklist and an afternoon seminar. This is not a knock on teachers and staff. It’s a gap in what schools have been asked and funded to provide.

Genuine school safety requires much more than a plan on paper. It means a strong physical footprint (single-point entry, rapid classroom door locks), modern safety tools (mass notification system, AI-assisted surveillance), and emergency training. Parents shouldn’t hesitate to ask direct questions. How are teachers trained? What safety tools are actually available in the classrooms? How quickly can the school communicate with families during an emergency? Teachers and staff deserve real support, and parents deserve transparency.

2. Talk about safety early — and often.

It’s a natural human instinct to want to shield a seven-year-old from a worry they haven’t asked for or to protect a college freshman’s first weeks from worst-case scenarios. I feel that pull every fall. But while it’s natural, it doesn’t protect our children from risk.

The goal isn’t to scare children. It’s to prepare them — to build awareness, confidence, and the ability to respond if something ever goes wrong. As parents, we can’t shy away from these discussions.

WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO

Obviously, what you say should be age-appropriate. The message you give a second-grader shouldn’t sound like the one you give a high school senior or college freshman.

For my wife and me, this meant walking through our kids’ schools ourselves, understanding the layout and emergency plans, then sitting down with our kids and having the conversation more than once. It’s not a one-time "big talk." It’s something we bring up naturally before school starts and revisit throughout the year. We remind them to pay attention to their surroundings, trust their instincts, and know what to do if something feels wrong.

Will older kids roll their eyes? Of course. "Yeah, mom. Yeah, dad. I know." That’s part of parenting. Say it anyway. Sometimes, the things our kids hear for the hundredth time are the things they remember when it matters most. And if they’re ever faced with danger, there’s a good chance they’ll remember exactly what you told them.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The same approach applies online. First-day-of-school photos are a tradition in our home, like many others. But we’ve started thinking twice before posting them. Sharing a school’s name, a daily routine, or a child’s interests online creates unnecessary exposure. Teaching our kids to pause before they post has become another safety habit we’re trying to build.

3. Evaluate appropriate personal safety tools.

Everyone has the right to feel safe, and families should take full advantage of every lawful tool their school or college permits. Families should familiarize themselves with campus policies and equip their students with the protective options they’re comfortable carrying. Depending on a student’s age and school policy, those options range from personal safety alarms to ballistic backpack inserts.

For college students, families should review campus safety policies and consider permitted personal safety tools — such as noise alarms, location-sharing emergency apps, and, where allowed by university policy, standard pepper spray. Faculty should consider other non-lethal options with greater range and stopping power.

We insure our homes against fires that may never happen. We buckle seat belts hoping they’ll never be needed. Preparing our children for a school emergency is no different. We all pray they’ll never have to use what we’ve taught them. But hope has never been a safety plan.

We can’t control every danger our children may face. We can control whether we’ve prepared them for it. That’s a responsibility no parent should leave to chance.

item.description: Caitlin Clark said it made her "a little sick" when Indiana Fever fans booed head coach Stephanie White during pregame introductions Tuesday night.
item.content:encoded:
Entering Tuesday's WNBA action, the Indiana Fever sat tied atop the Eastern Conference standings at 20-12 on the year. The team also happens to lead the league in points scored per game with the two-headed monster of Kelsey Mitchell and Caitlin Clark leading the charge.

Overall, things should be pretty great for Fever head coach Stephanie White and her squad with the WNBA playoffs in sight.

In reality, the situation in Indiana is completely unsettled, and White was reminded of that on Tuesday night when some fans booed her during pregame introductions ahead of the Fever's home contest against the New York Liberty.

FEVER COACH STEPHANIE WHITE LAUNCHES FIERY DEFENSE OF HERSELF AFTER SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM HIT

Clark addressed the boos her head coach received during her postgame press conference following Indiana's 106-92 win, and she was none too pleased.

"I hated that our fans booed her before the game," Clark explained. "That made me a little sick, to be honest. We're going to ride for her, and we're always going to have her back," Clark continued. "That's never going to tear our locker room apart."

White hearing some boos while being introduced in her own team's building came shortly after she delivered quite the pregame rant about Indiana's Sophie Cunningham and the hard foul she took over the weekend from Chicago's DiJonai Carrington, and the overall boiling tensions around the league.

White explained Tuesday that she didn't, in real time, get to see replays of the foul that left Cunningham with a bloody mouth and Carrington being ejected from the game before going directly to her postgame press conference.

"Was it egregious? Absolutely," White said. "When you have a chance to watch that over and over and over on replay, you can see that. I didn't have that in real time."

CAITLIN CLARK, KELSEY MITCHELL POWER FEVER PAST LIBERTY, LIFT INDIANA ATOP EASTERN CONFERENCE

LONG LIST OF EMBARRASSING WNBA INCIDENTS IS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN SPORTS LEAGUES MADE POLITICS THEIR PRIMARY FOCUS

White then took offense to anyone suggesting that she didn't have her players’ backs and addressed the "online community" that she accused of creating what she believes are false narratives.

"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win," White said. "It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided."

White closed out her pregame presser on Tuesday by saying critics can "go to hell."

"Love will win, grace will win. Humility will win, and kindness will win. I stand by them, I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell," an emotional White said.

While White admitted that she wasn't able to see replays of Carrington's Flagrant 2 foul on Cunningham from the Fever's game against the Sky on Saturday, that didn't stop her from essentially defending Carrington during her postgame press conference following the contest on Aug. 8.

"Yeah, I mean, look, it was a hard foul. I don't think that DiJonai intentionally came out to get her across the neck like she did. But it did happen, and I thought it was the right call," White said.

"But you know, one of the things about Nay is that she's gonna play her butt off, man. She's gonna compete. Nobody's gonna go walking in for a layup. And so, I don't oppose the hard foul. But I also don't think that she intentionally went for the neck."

Over the span of about 72 hours, White failed to stand up for her own player in Cunningham following the foul, walked back her initial comments about Carrington's foul while admitting she didn't replay the play in real time yet came to a conclusion, and told critics they could go to hell.

Fever fans feeling a sense of frustration with the head coach is understandable.

item.title: Fake rental listing scams can cost you thousands
item.description: FBI real estate fraud complaints jumped from 9,359 in 2024 to 12,368 in 2025 as fake rental listing scams grow more convincing with stolen photos.
item.content:encoded:
You find a charming rental in the right neighborhood. The price sits slightly below other homes nearby. Better yet, it becomes available right when your current lease ends. Then the pressure begins. Consider a Southern California renter who recently found a two-bedroom bungalow near family. The supposed landlord said she could not tour it because the current occupants had not moved out. Instead, he sent her a professional video of the home.

The video looked convincing because it was real. However, the scammer had copied it from an earlier property listing. After collecting an application fee, the fake landlord requested a deposit through Zelle. A phone conversation helped ease the renter's concerns. He also promised receipts and said the deposit was refundable.

She sent more than $2,500. When she asked for the money back, the calls stopped and the messages went unanswered. The actual homeowner still lived in the house and had never offered it for rent. That experience shows how quickly fake rental listing scams can turn a hopeful move into a financial crisis.
